title: Tea May Benefit Heart Health — If It's Not Too Hot
paragraphs: Tea is one of the most popular drinks in the world, and many studies have suggested that it may be good for the heart. However, according to a large new study from China, how hot people drink their tea may make a big difference.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Internal Medicine in October 2026, looked at more than 485,000 adults in China aged between 30 and 79. The participants answered questions about how often they drank tea, which type they preferred, how strong it was and how hot they drank it. The researchers then followed them for about nine years on average. During that time, there were more than 14,800 cases of heart and blood vessel disease, including heart attacks and strokes.

The researchers found that people who drank tea at least three days a week had about an 11% lower risk of these diseases than people who drank it less often. Both black and green tea were linked to benefits, but black tea was linked to a lower risk of more types of disease.

However, temperature mattered. People who drank their tea at room temperature, or hot but not scalding, had a significantly lower risk than people who did not drink tea regularly. In contrast, people who drank their tea "burning hot" had a 16% higher risk.
The lowest risk was seen among people who drank about six to eight cups a day. However, the researchers warned that people should not see this as a recommended amount.
There were also some limitations. The study was observational, and people reported their own habits. For example, people may have different ideas about what "burning hot" means.

Dr. Leana Wen, an emergency physician, advises people to let their tea cool until they can drink it comfortably. She points out that regularly drinking very hot drinks has been linked to cancer of the esophagus.
